newsitem.title: UK: UK govt unveils insurance scheme for elderly.
newsitem.headline: UK govt unveils insurance scheme for elderly.

text.p: British Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell on Monday unveiled plans to offer private insurance for residential care for the elderly, another plank in the government's pre-election shake-up of social services.
Dorrell said the new plan would remove the threat of old people having to give up large chunks of their life savings or even their homes to pay for long-term care in nursing homes.
Up to now Britons needing long-term care have had to use their own funds until their assets fall to 16,000 pounds ($25,700), at which point the state will step in to help them.

The new scheme -- "A New Partership for Care in Old Age" -- offers a partnership insurance scheme. For every one pound the insurance scheme pays out, people will be able to keep 1.50 pounds more of their capital than the current means test allows.
In other words, taking out the insurance raises the 16,000 pounds level under which state help is not offered.

"People who have worked hard and saved for the future not only want to retain their independence with regard to provision of their social care, they also want to pass on more of their savings and other assets to their children," Dorrell said.
"What we are announcing today is more generous support for those who take out insurance to cover this kind of cost for themselves."

Dorrell said it would be for insurers to decide what to charge different individuals for insurance. Under the scheme, insurance premiums will be paid into a pool with only those who need social care drawing money out.

Since not everbody will need care, those who do will be able to pay for it at less cost to themselves. Those who do not need care still have the peace of mind from knowing they are covered, a government document said.
Dorrell said the care plans would not, even in the long-run, cost the government more than 200 million pounds a year.
The plans formed part of a paper the government will release later this week, setting out the future for social services.
Last week, Social Security Secretary Peter Lilley announced plans to shake-up pensions, with part of people's national insurance contributions to be paid into private funds to invest on their behalf.

The proposals are widely seen as an attempt to convince the British electorate that the government can still come up with big ideas. It faces an election, probably on May 1, and trails the opposition Labour Party by about 20 points in the polls.

Dorrell said the residential care scheme would also allow people to top up the amount spent on their care, over and above the amount that local authorities deem necessary, an option not allowed up to now.
"In a free society social care is something people should plan and cater for themselves," he said. "But of course, the government will provide a safety net for those who find it impossible."
